where [MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]] and [MATH: [y_{1}; y_{2}]]

Content:
How do we express [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})] in terms of the components of [MATH: \mathbf{y}?]

Content:
First, notice that

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
gives the following expressions for [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2\mathbin{:}]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we are given a quadratic form

Content:
[MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{x}]

Content:
and an invertible matrix [MATH: P] that defines the change of variable

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
If this change of variable is applied to the quadratic form [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}),] what will be the new matrix of [MATH: Q]?

Content:
By making the necessary substitutions, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: Q(x)|= x^{T}Ax; = (Py)^{T}A(Py); = y^{T}P^{T}APy; = y^{T}(P^{T}AP)y]

Content:
Therefore, the new matrix of our quadratic form is

Content:
[MATH: B= P^T \! A P.]

[MATH: [1|− 2; − 2|0]]

[MATH: [1|− 2; − 2|0]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T] is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and [MATH: \mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T] is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of [MATH: P,] then

[MATH: \mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: x^{T}Ax|= (Py)^{T}A(Py); = (y^{T}P^{T})A(Py); = y^{T}(P^{T}AP)y,]

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

[MATH: P^{T}AP|= [− 1|2; − 1|1]^{T}[1|− 2; − 2|0][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [− 1|− 1; 2|1][1|− 2; − 2|0][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [1|2; 0|− 4][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [− 3|4; 4|− 4]]

[MATH: Q(x)|= x_{1}x_{2} + 2x_{2}^{2}; = (− y_{2})(− y_{1} − 2y_{2}) + 2(− y_{1} − 2y_{2})^{2}; = y_{2}y_{1} + 2y_{2}^{2} + 2y_{1}^{2} + 8y_{1}y_{2} + 8y_{2}^{2}; = 2y_{1}^{2} + 9y_{1}y_{2} + 10y_{2}^{2}]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Connection Between Matrices of Quadratic Forms in Different Bases

Content:
Suppose we are given a quadratic form

Content:
[MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{x}]

Content:
and an invertible matrix [MATH: P] that defines the change of variable

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
If this change of variable is applied to the quadratic form [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}),] what will be the new matrix of [MATH: Q]?

Content:
By making the necessary substitutions, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: Q(x)|= x^{T}Ax; = (Py)^{T}A(Py); = y^{T}P^{T}APy; = y^{T}(P^{T}AP)y]

Content:
Therefore, the new matrix of our quadratic form is

Content:
[MATH: B= P^T \! A P.]

Item 9 — Example: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

Example Prompt:

[MATH: [1|− 2; − 2|0]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T] is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and [MATH: \mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T] is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of [MATH: P,] then

[MATH: \mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: x^{T}Ax|= (Py)^{T}A(Py); = (y^{T}P^{T})A(Py); = y^{T}(P^{T}AP)y,]

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

[MATH: P^{T}AP|= [− 1|2; − 1|1]^{T}[1|− 2; − 2|0][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [− 1|− 1; 2|1][1|− 2; − 2|0][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [1|2; 0|− 4][− 1|2; − 1|1]; = [− 3|4; 4|− 4]]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Equivalent Quadratic Forms

Content:
Two quadratic forms [MATH: Q_1] and [MATH: Q_2] on [MATH: \Bbb R^n] are said to be equivalent if they can be obtained from each other through a change of variable.

Content:
> The two quadratic forms with matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are equivalent if and only if there exists an invertible matrix [MATH: P] such that [MATH: B = P^T \! A \, P.]

Content:
Note: Equivalent quadratic forms represent the same function from [MATH: \Bbb R^n] to [MATH: \Bbb R.]
